title: Multi-Platform Image Builds
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of multi-platform image builds.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to multi-platform image builds.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Multi-Platform Image Builds. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Modern Docker builds use BuildKit capabilities for cache-aware build graphs, stage selection, secret mounts, and multi-platform output. A build cache is an optimization rather than a trust boundary; keep credentials out of image layers and validate the exact builder/driver and output behavior. Learning multi-platform image builds helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Multi-Platform Image Builds
content_blocks.code:
docker buildx version
docker buildx ls
# Example shape (requires an authorized registry and configured builder):
# docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --tag REGISTRY/IMAGE:VERSION --push .
content_blocks.expected_output: The first commands show Buildx availability and builders. The commented command describes a multi-platform publish and needs a real authorized registry/tag.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run the two inspection commands first. Treat the build/push example as a plan until your builder, target platforms, and registry permissions have been checked.
content_blocks.reset_steps: The inspection commands are read-only. A pushed image is a registry side effect and should be done only in a test repository.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
